name: Induction cut

card.summary: A uniform, very short clipper cut given to military recruits that is also chosen as a minimal, low-maintenance look.

quick.overview:
The induction cut clips all hair to the same stubble length, around 1/16 to 1/8 inch by one account, with no fade or styling. It exposes hairline, head shape and scalp.

People choose it for a clean look with almost no upkeep, and some use it to manage thinning or receding hair by removing contrast between thick and sparse areas.
quick.how: It is done with clippers, either guardless or on the shortest setting, across the whole head. Regrowth shows quickly, so people re-clip regularly to keep it uniform.
quick.risks: Little risk beyond razor-type irritation and sunburn on an exposed scalp. It shows head shape and scalp blemishes, which some people dislike.

lead: The induction cut is the uniform haircut given to new military recruits, clipped to a stubble length across the whole head.[1] Grokipedia describes it as shorter than typical guard-based buzz cuts but not a full shave.[1]

Outside the military it works as a minimal haircut. Wikipedia notes that buzz cuts in general are low maintenance and can make the face look more defined and suit people with thinning or receding hairlines.[2]

chain: Removes visible contrast of thinning areas
Emphasises face and head shape with minimal upkeep
angle.text: People pick the cut to look neat with no styling effort and to conceal uneven thinning. It also puts focus on facial structure and skull shape.

infobox: Clippers, no guard or lowest setting

paras: Grokipedia describes it as uniform stubble across the scalp with no parting or tapering, differing from crew cuts (longer on top) and high-and-tight cuts (shaved sides).[1]

Short military cuts were adopted to prevent head lice, and the practice persists for ease of maintenance, cooling and uniformity.[2] Clippers popularised in the late 19th century made such cuts quick to produce.[2]
